Labeled break and continue statements can target an enclosing labeled loop or switch, simplifying control flow in nested loops.
`lock` on a statically typed `System.Threading.Lock` lowers through `EnterScope` and scope disposal; a `lock` body still cannot use `await`.
Iterator methods may contain unsafe blocks, but `yield` statements must remain in a safe context. Ref locals and ref struct locals may be used when they do not cross a yield boundary.
C# 8 introduced using declarations, await using, and await foreach; these language forms use synchronous or asynchronous disposal/enumeration patterns.

accuracyFacts: C# 15 labeled break can target an enclosing loop or switch; labeled continue can target only an enclosing loop. C# 15 feature status checked against current Microsoft language documentation.

`yield return` and `yield break` cannot appear in catch/finally clauses or a try with a catch; both are permitted in try-finally without catch, and starting C# 13 iterator methods may include unsafe blocks but yield statements must be in safe context.
C# 13 allows ref/ref struct locals in iterator methods only when those values do not cross yield boundaries.
An exception filter runs before stack unwinding. A filter that evaluates false or itself throws is treated as not matching.
`using` and `await using` support appropriate disposal patterns as well as interface-based disposal; declarations dispose at the end of their enclosing scope.
A `lock` body cannot contain await. .NET 9/C# 13 uses `System.Threading.Lock.EnterScope` lowering when that is the static type of the lock expression.

checked/unchecked statements affect specified integral arithmetic and conversions that are textually within the context. Called method bodies are not affected; division by zero still throws in unchecked context.
Expression statements are restricted to permitted statement-expression forms; a semicolon does not turn every expression into a valid statement.
A goto target must be valid within the current function and respect local-variable scope and definite-assignment rules.
